\chapter{Saying Who You Are}
\label{ch:zh-mingzi}
\hlchaptermodality{8}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can write \zh{我}, \zh{名} and \zh{字}, introduce myself with \zh{我是} and my own name, recognise \zh{名字} as the word for a name, and I know that Mandarin words never change shape for grammar.}

The first exchange the reader cannot finish without supplying something of their own -- their name -- and the first place the book names a gap it is choosing not to fill, rather than teaching a sentence no speaker would say.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[wǒ]{\zh{我} — seven strokes, and an honest admission}

\label{lesson:ZH-W08-wo}



\begin{quote}
Write \zh{是}. Nine strokes, sun finished on top.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — the shape}
\begin{quote}
\zh{我}
\end{quote}

\textbf{Seven strokes}, and here this book owes you a straight answer.

Every character so far has come apart into pieces you already had: \zh{你} into \zh{亻} and \zh{尔}, \zh{是} into \zh{日} and a body, \zh{早} into \zh{日} and \zh{十}. \textbf{\zh{我} does not.} Its right side is a shape called \zh{戈} — there it is, but naming it is all this lesson will do with it, because you have not been taught to write it. Its left side is a squeezed hand. Neither is a piece you own.

So learn it as a \textbf{route}, not as a sum. Follow the order and it holds together:

1. a short \textbf{falling stroke} at the upper left 2. the \textbf{upper horizontal}, left to right 3. the \textbf{vertical}, coming down and \textbf{hooking left} without lifting 4. the \textbf{lower rising stroke} 5. the \textbf{long curved slash} down to the right, \textbf{hooking upward} at its end 6. a separate \textbf{rising slash} up to the left 7. a \textbf{dot} at the upper right, pressed down-right

Six pen lifts.

Two of these are joined strokes that must not be broken: \textbf{stroke 3} (down, then hook) and \textbf{stroke 5} (the long slash, then hook up). Everything you have learned about turning strokes applies here — the pen changes direction, the stroke does not end.

The dot goes \textbf{last}. Small marks at the upper right are finishers, and you will see that again.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Write it:} \zh{我} slowly, twice — and keep strokes 3 and 5 unbroken
  \item \emph{Write it:} \zh{我} once more, saving the dot for last
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{wǒ} — low and dipping
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Is this character built from pieces you already know? (\textbf{No} — and this book would rather say so than invent a story.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U4E00.pdf}{Unicode CJK Unified Ideographs chart}; stroke order per the PRC standard \emph{Xiandai Hanyu Tongyongzi Bishun Guifan} (1997).
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[wǒ]{\zh{我} — I, me, and saying who you are}

\label{lesson:ZH-C08-wo}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{wǒ}. Low and dipping, and hold the bottom of it.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\zh{我}} \emph{wǒ} — \textbf{I}. And also \textbf{me}.

English uses two words there and swaps between them depending on the job: \emph{I saw her}, \emph{she saw me}. \textbf{Mandarin uses \zh{我} for both}, and this is your first sight of something that will save you a great deal of work: \textbf{Mandarin words do not change shape for grammar.} No endings, no cases, no agreement. \zh{我} is \zh{我} wherever it stands.

Now put it to work with a word you already have:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\zh{我是}} \emph{wǒ shì} — \textbf{I am}
\end{quote}

\zh{是} is the word you learned for answering yes. Its actual job is to link two things: \textbf{\zh{我是}} and then who you are. Say your own name after it and you have introduced yourself.

Two third tones meet in \emph{wǒ shì}? No — \zh{是} is \textbf{fourth} tone. Nothing moves.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{wǒ}, then \textbf{wǒ shì} — low and dipping, then falling
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{wǒ shì} followed by your own name, out loud, twice
  \item \emph{Write it:} \zh{我是}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \zh{是} do in \zh{我是}? (\textbf{It links you to whatever comes next}.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U4E00.pdf}{Unicode CJK Unified Ideographs chart}
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[míng]{\zh{名} — a mouth with something above it}

\label{lesson:ZH-W08-ming}



\begin{quote}
Write \zh{口}. Three strokes, and the box is not closed until the last one.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — the shape}
\begin{quote}
\zh{名}
\end{quote}

\textbf{Six strokes}, and three of them are \zh{口}, which you already own.

\textbf{\zh{名} is \zh{夕} sitting on top of \zh{口}.} The lower half is the mouth. The upper half is \textbf{\zh{夕}}, a shape this book has not taught you as a character of its own — here it is a piece, and naming it is enough:

1. \textbf{\zh{夕}'s upper falling stroke}, down to the left 2. \textbf{\zh{夕}'s horizontal}, continuing \textbf{down-left without lifting} — one stroke 3. \textbf{\zh{夕}'s inner dot}, pressed down-right 4-6. \textbf{\zh{口}, complete.} Left side; top and right in one turning stroke; the bottom bar closing it.

Five pen lifts.

\textbf{Finish \zh{夕} before you begin \zh{口}} — the same instinct as finishing \zh{日} before the body of \zh{是}, and finishing the sun before \zh{十} in \zh{早}. You have now met that rule often enough that it should feel like the obvious thing to do.

A hook worth having, offered as a hook: \zh{夕} is the shape used for \textbf{evening}, and a mouth beneath it reads easily as \textbf{speaking your name in the dark, when you cannot be seen}. That is a traditional story, not proven history — but \zh{名} does mean \textbf{name}, and the picture makes the character stick.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Write it:} \zh{口} alone, then \zh{名} — and notice the last three strokes are identical
  \item \emph{Write it:} \zh{名} again, keeping stroke 2 unbroken
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{míng} — rising
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which half goes first? (\textbf{The top} — as always.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U4E00.pdf}{Unicode CJK Unified Ideographs chart}; stroke order per the PRC standard \emph{Xiandai Hanyu Tongyongzi Bishun Guifan} (1997).
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[zì]{\zh{字} — a child under a roof}

\label{lesson:ZH-W08-zi}



\begin{quote}
Write \zh{子}, the child — the piece that stands beside \zh{女} in \zh{好}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — the shape}
\begin{quote}
\zh{字}
\end{quote}

\textbf{Six strokes}, and the bottom three are \zh{子}, which you have written since the first chapter.

\textbf{\zh{字} is \zh{子} under a roof.} The roof is \textbf{\zh{宀}}, a piece rather than a character — three strokes that make a lid:

1. \textbf{\zh{宀}'s top dot}, pressed down-right 2. \textbf{\zh{宀}'s left side}, a short stroke down-left 3. \textbf{\zh{宀}'s horizontal roof}, running right and \textbf{hooking down-left} at its end — one stroke 4-6. \textbf{\zh{子}, complete.} Its top horizontal turning down-left; its vertical with a left hook; its middle horizontal last.

Five pen lifts.

\textbf{Roof before child.} A covering piece is finished before whatever sits under it, which is the same habit as \zh{日} before the body of \zh{是} and \zh{夕} before \zh{口} in \zh{名}.

And now the meaning, which is the reason this character is worth the effort. \textbf{\zh{字}} \emph{zì} means \textbf{character} — a written Chinese character. It is the word for the thing you have been learning to make since the first page of this book. The roof-and-child picture is the traditional hook: something raised and kept under shelter.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Write it:} \zh{子} alone, then \zh{字} — the difference is a roof
  \item \emph{Write it:} \zh{字}, saying \textquotedblleft{}roof first\textquotedblright{} before you start
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{zì} — falling
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which goes first, the roof or the child? (\textbf{The roof}.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U4E00.pdf}{Unicode CJK Unified Ideographs chart}; stroke order per the PRC standard \emph{Xiandai Hanyu Tongyongzi Bishun Guifan} (1997).
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[míngzi]{\zh{名字} — the word for a name}

\label{lesson:ZH-C08-mingzi}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{zǎoshang}. Second syllable light and short.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\zh{名字}} \emph{míngzi} — \textbf{name}.

Both halves are characters you have just written, and both mean something:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\zh{名}} \emph{míng} — \textbf{name}
  \item \textbf{\zh{字}} \emph{zì} — \textbf{character}, a written unit
\end{itemize}

So the word is \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}name-character\textquotedblright{}}, and that is not a stretched hook. A Chinese personal name \emph{is} a small number of characters, usually two or three, each chosen deliberately for what it means. The word for \textquotedblleft{}name\textquotedblright{} says what a name is made of.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{sounds}
\emph{míngzi}, not \emph{míngzì}.

\textbf{\zh{字}} is fourth tone standing alone, and you practised it that way — but in this word it goes \textbf{neutral}, short and light, exactly as \zh{上} did inside \zh{早上}. Second syllables do this often, and you now know the signal: \textbf{no tone mark means no tone.}

\emph{míng} rises; \emph{zi} rides on the end of it. {[}REPEAT x2{]}
\end{sounds}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{zì} alone, falling — then \textbf{míngzi}, with the second syllable light
  \item \textbf{míngzi} twice, and say what each of its two halves means
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which syllable of \emph{míngzi} carries no tone? (\textbf{The second}.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U4E00.pdf}{Unicode CJK Unified Ideographs chart}
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Practice — saying who you are}

\label{lesson:ZH-C08-practice}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{wǒ shì} — low and dipping, then falling.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The exchange}
Two people meet in the morning. The gap in the third line is yours to fill.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{A:} \zh{早上好}
\end{quote}

>

\begin{quote}
\emph{zǎoshang hǎo} — good morning.
\end{quote}

>

\begin{quote}
\textbf{B:} \zh{早上好}
\end{quote}

>

\begin{quote}
\emph{zǎoshang hǎo} — good morning.
\end{quote}

>

\begin{quote}
\textbf{A:} \zh{我是} …
\end{quote}

>

\begin{quote}
\emph{wǒ shì …} — I am … (your name).
\end{quote}

>

\begin{quote}
\textbf{B:} \zh{我是} …
\end{quote}

>

\begin{quote}
\emph{wǒ shì …} — I am … (their name).
\end{quote}

>

\begin{quote}
\textbf{A:} \zh{再见}
\end{quote}

>

\begin{quote}
\emph{zàijiàn} — goodbye.
\end{quote}

Say it with your own name in it, out loud. That is the first time this book has asked you for something it could not supply.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built — and one thing deliberately withheld}]
You can now greet by time of day, say who you are, and leave. Every line is built from characters you have written.

One honest gap, and it is worth naming rather than hiding. You have the word for \textbf{name} — \zh{名字} — but not yet the way to \textbf{ask} for someone's. The natural Mandarin question needs a word this book has not given you, and asking it with only the pieces you have would mean teaching you a sentence a speaker would not say. It is coming, and it is worth waiting for.

What \zh{名字} buys you now is real: you can recognise the word when someone else uses it, and you know that a name is \textbf{characters} — which is why a Chinese speaker asked about their name will often tell you which characters it uses.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{wǒ shì}, then your own name, three times
  \item \emph{Say it:} the whole exchange, taking both parts
  \item \emph{Write it:} \zh{我是}, then \zh{名字}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Can you yet ask someone else for their name? (\textbf{Not yet} — and the book would rather say so than hand you a sentence nobody says.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U4E00.pdf}{Unicode CJK Unified Ideographs chart}
\end{tcolorbox}
